WHY HEIRS GIVE UP Five portals, one grieving family 1 UDGAM (RBI): unclaimed bank deposits 2 MITRA (SEBI): inactive mutual fund investments 3 Bima Bharosa (IRDAI): insurance 4 IEPF (MCA): shares and unpaid dividends 5 EPFO: provident fund The core problem: heirs often don't know an asset exists, so they don't know which portal to search. The PIL asks for one search, by the deceased person's name, across all of them. Adv. Ashwani Kumar 03 / 08

Who should be able to search a dead person's money? THE RISK DESIGN THAT ANSWERS IT A name-searchable list is a gift Search unlocked by a death to impostors certificate plus the claimant's The Centre raised privacy and KYC misuse concerns Show only where an asset is In March, the Court called a held, not the balance relaxed claims process Logged searches; claims still "absolutely preposterous" verified by the institution because of fraud risk Privacy is a reason to design the registry carefully, not a reason to leave ₹1 lakh crore with no way for heirs to find it. Don't wait for the judgment ✓ Add nominees everywhere: bank accounts, demat, mutual fund folios, insurance, EPF. Banks now allow up to four. ✓ Keep an asset list: institution and account type, kept where your family can find it. ✓ Search for a late relative: UDGAM lets you select all banks; check MITRA and the IEPF portal too. ✓ Your data, too: Section 14 of the DPDP Act will let you nominate someone to exercise your data rights after death, once it comes into force on 13 May 2027. Adv. Ashwani Kumar 07 / 08

A deadline the government set for itself should not need a court order. Separate portals put the burden on grieving families to already know what to look for. A single registry with verified, logged access can protect privacy and still let heirs find what is theirs. Whatever the Court orders, it should set a timeline. Adv.
